title: In a hurry
hook: seminary students hurrying to talk about the Good Samaritan often passed a person in need (Darley and Batson)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the seat. A waiting room, a woman on crutches, and meditators who stood up. Did you give up a seat or a spot? Day one thousand three hundred nine.

"A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves." That's how Jesus begins the parable of the Good Samaritan, in the Gospel of Luke, as the King James Version has it. Robbed, beaten, left half dead by the road. A priest comes by and passes on the other side. A Levite does the same. Then a Samaritan, a traveler from Samaria, stops, binds his wounds, and pays for his care. Some readers ask why the first two walked past. A pair of psychologists decided to find out what might make anyone walk past.
screen: `FELL AMONG THIEVES.` → `TWO PASS BY.` → `ONE STOPS.` → `WHY DO PEOPLE WALK PAST?`

segments.voice: First, the setup. John Darley and Daniel Batson recruited students at a theological seminary. Each was asked to prepare a short talk. Some got a talk on jobs for ministers. Some got the parable of the Good Samaritan itself. Then each was sent across campus to give it in another building. Second, the clock. Before they left, some were told they were late and had to hurry. Others were told they had a few minutes, or plenty of time. Third, the man in the doorway. On the way, each student passed a man slumped in an alley, head down, coughing and groaning. He was part of the study. The question was simple: who stops? Fourth, the answer. The students in a hurry stopped far less often than the ones with time. And here's the sting: the topic of the talk made little difference. Students on their way to speak about the Good Samaritan were not much more likely to help than the others. The researchers reported that on some occasions, a student hurrying to talk about the parable literally stepped over the man to get there. The parable never says why the priest and the Levite passed by. The study doesn't claim to know either. But it raises a plain possibility: not hard hearts, just full calendars. So the week ends here. A week about compassion as something real and trainable ends with a very ordinary obstacle. Not cruelty. Hurry.
screen: `A TALK ON THE GOOD SAMARITAN.` · `SOME TOLD THEY WERE LATE.` · then, large: `A MAN SLUMPED IN A DOORWAY.` · then: `HURRY, NOT THE TOPIC.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave five minutes early. Sit, and let the breath slow down on its own. Then look at the rest of today. Find one trip, one meeting, one pickup where you usually arrive just in time, or a little late. Decide now to leave five minutes earlier for it. Picture those spare minutes on the way: room to notice a face, a dropped bag, a person who looks lost. Then rest in the breath, in no hurry at all. The bell holds the time.
In a hurry. In one study, seminary students rushing to talk about the Good Samaritan often passed a man in need; hurry mattered more than the topic. Today's word.
Your line: not in a hurry. Today, leave five minutes early for one thing, and spend the spare minutes looking up instead of down. Day one thousand three hundred nine.

howItsDone: Christians read the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10) as a teaching about who counts as a neighbor; some people build slack into their day on purpose, leaving early so there's room to notice and help.

fork.reveal: students in a hurry stopped far less often, even those about to speak on the parable itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: people pass by someone in need because they don't care.
what it means: in Darley and Batson's study, being in a hurry made people far less likely to stop.
what a scholar hears: the topic of the talk barely mattered, which suggests the situation, not the sermon in someone's head, often decides who helps.
